title: Playing Play, Fiddle, Play and the conventional highest bass notes
summary: After an on-tape performance, Stewart says conventional bass stopped near G because higher sounds like a cello, so the high notes were his gimmick.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: (Musical interlude.)
Higher.
Higher?
Uh-huh, go higher.
You mean to tell me you want me to go higher?
Uh-huh.
Okay. (Singing), Please excuse me and forgive me. Please help me, we'll try to do better next time to reach that high note. When we try to play, play fiddle, play fiddle, play.
Well, there we had "Play, Fiddle, Play."
Now that was that -- we heard that famous 'squeak D' there.
That's right, yes.
Right. So now when you were studying the bass in those years, what was the conventional -- what was about the highest note for the conventional technique of the bass at that time?
Well, at that time, if I were to go up to around the -- let's say a G. (Plays note.)
Uh-huh.
Around there, would be more or less high enough in order to stay in the bass range, you know. Why play a whole lot of notes above G when it will tend to sound more like a cello?
Uh-huh. But when you did 'Play, Fiddle, Play,' though, you went beyond the cello range.
Oh, yes, I did. That was my -- what would you call it? My little gimmick.
Tour de force.
There you go.
(Laughter.)
Now, in terms of plucking, what was about the highest note that the guys played in those --
Well, around the G, more or less. (Playing bass.) If I go up a little high, I'll get up into almost a D. (Playing bass.)
